Recognized through lectures, competitions, and exhibitions, the approach positions AI as accountable architectural intelligence.

item.title: Murder Beneath the Masterpiece
item.content:encoded: In a locked attic room, the portrait’s grotesque transformation is exposed, proving that every sin has scarred the once-beautiful image. Horrified, the painter urges repentance, but pride and hatred overwhelm his friend. In a sudden frenzy, he murders him to protect the secret. item.title: AI Malware That Rewrites Its Own Code Is Emerging as a Major Cybersecurity Threat in 2026
item.content:encoded: New generation of malware can rewrite parts of its own code automatically. It can evolve during an attack and evade many conventional security tools. Security analysts say this capability significantly weakens signature-based antivirus systems.

item.title: AI Startups Don’t Die From Moving Slow. They Die From Moving Blind
item.content:encoded: AI startups fail not from moving too slowly, but from moving blindly—building products that lose relevance due to rapid model advancements or solving problems that aren’t painful enough to sustain demand. Speed is important, but it’s useless if the product lacks staying power or solves a shallow problem. Founders often mistake early traction (curiosity, demos, investor interest) for real demand, committing resources to weak assumptions that become hard to reverse. To succeed, startups must focus on three critical factors: Speed × Truth × Staying Power. They should ask: What remains unique if the underlying model improves? Does the product solve a painful, hard-to-ignore problem? What assumptions are they unwilling to question? The key is to build products that are inconvenient to replace, not just clever or novel, and to continuously pressure-test assumptions before they become costly to change.

item.title: Kill Heroes, Build Systems and Processes

item.title: Java Under the Hood - Dive Into JVM Memory Model and Garbage Collector
item.content:encoded:
Java abstracts away manual memory management, but the JVM still operates on a precise memory model. Local variables and method frames live on the stack, while actual objects live on the heap, which is divided into generations to make garbage collection efficient. Different reference types (strong, soft, weak, phantom) influence GC behavior, especially for caches and off-heap resources. Garbage Collection uses variations of mark-and-sweep to identify reachable objects and reclaim memory from the rest, sometimes compacting to avoid fragmentation. GC pauses are real and can impact latency, which is why selecting the right collector matters (G1, Parallel, ZGC, Shenandoah, etc.) and why JVM tuning exists. Understanding how memory works under the hood enables developers to diagnose leaks, reduce allocation pressure, tune pause times, and configure the JVM for different workloads — turning memory management from a black box into a performance tool.
